title: Bridging the Industrial Productivity Gap: An Engineering Perspective on Manufacturing Capacity and Performance in Zimbabwe
content: Despite the fact that manufacturing has been observed to be a force of productivity growth and structural change in developing economies, its performance in Zimbabwe has not been given due attention in the last decade with the exception of one or two anecdotal studies albeit in a qualitative manner. This study examines the sector’s contribution to the national output and constraints which affect it from 2014 to 2023. Using World Bank national-accounts data, the Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries (CZI) annual manufacturing survey, a structured literature synthesis and a structured questionnaire of the industry, we investigate manufacturing value added (MVA), capacity utilisation, employment and import dependence. MVA’s share of GDP was not a consistent trend, but was seen to be the lowest around 11% during 2017, highest around 21.5% during 2022, and lowest around 13.8% during 2023, with the sector’s poorest relative position corresponding to the 2019–2020 economic contraction. Since 2009, capacity utilisation has been between 32% and 57%, meaning there was 43.9% of the installed capacity that was not being used in 2022, and manufacturers import about 45% of their inputs, largely because they are not available domestically. The key constraints that are identified are the electricity supply of 1272 MW, compared to the demand of 2100 MW, the damage to transport and water infrastructure, the policy instability and exposure to exchange-rate movement. We do not believe that the problem is how big industry is in Zimbabwe, but how much of its capacity is being used and the depth of local input supply, as well as export competitiveness and policy predictability, and we begin to enlist a few priorities to address the manufacturing challenge in this country.
